implementation_notes: SpriteKit supplies the frame hook: 'Do not call this method directly; it is called by the system exactly once per frame, so long as the scene is presented in a view and is not paused. This is the first method called when animating the scene, before any actions are evaluated and before any physics are simulated', and Apple documents it as 'the primary place to implement your own in-game simulation, including input handling, artificial intelligence, game scripting'. What replaces the classic structure: the presented scene is the collection and the engine is the driver, so your entities are walked inside update(_:) (or you subclass SKNode and dispatch from the scene). The hand-written entity list remains the right shape for a custom renderer, where nothing provides the hook.
pitfalls: currentTime is the system time, so the first call yields a huge delta; clamp and initialise it instead of stepping by the raw difference.
A paused scene stops calling update, which stops every per-object step: pausing gameplay by pausing the scene is usually right, but it hides 'frozen object' bugs.
Physics and SKActions already advance inside the frame, so stepping them again from update double-integrates motion.
update runs on the render thread: long work drops frames, so keep per-step work bounded and move heavy computation off it.

variants.name: GameplayKit per-component update dispatch
variants.implementation_notes: GameplayKit packages the per-object dispatch: a GKComponentSystem 'manages periodic update messages for components in a game that uses Entity-Component architecture' and 'forwards to the update(deltaTime:) method of all the GKComponent subclass instances it manages, allowing those objects to perform per-frame update logic'. GameplayKit offers two shapes - per-entity (call each entity's update, which forwards to its components) or per-component (component systems called from the scene's frame method, 'without traversing your game's object hierarchy to dispatch update messages'). What replaces the classic structure: the component system is the collection and the framework performs the walk; you register components and call system.update(deltaTime:) from update(_:) or a display link. Choose it when entities are component bags and per-component-class ordering matters; a plain list walk stays simpler for small games.
pitfalls: A component only updates while registered with a system: forgetting addComponent(foundIn:) leaves it silently inert.
Per-component order is the order in which the systems are called, not the entity list, so dependencies between component classes must be expressed by that call order.
GKComponent.update(deltaTime:) is called by the system; calling it yourself double-steps the component.
